paragraphs: Each subject executed the tasks lifting a load using both hands (i.e. S05_Lift_LI1_1 where 5 is the number of the subject, LI1 is the level of risk, _1 is the number of repetition).
The lifting tasks were executed at three different risk levels.

The three lifting risk conditions were determined according to the Revised NIOSH Lifting Equation (Waters et al., 1993, 1994). The three lifting risk conditions were chosen to obtain Lifting Index (LI) values of 1, 2, and 3 (Table 1). LI is calculated as the ratio between the load weight (L) and the Recommended Weight Limit (RWL) expressed by the following equations (Waters et al., 1993, 1994):
RWL=LC x HM x VM x DM x AM x FM x CM

where the Load Costant (LC, 23 kg) is weighted by the Horizontal (HM), Vertical (VM), Vertical Travel Distance (DM), Asymmetry Angle (AM), lifting frequency (FM) and Hand-to-object Coupling (CM) Multipliers. The multipliers were rated on the following parameters respectively: horizontal (H) and vertical (V) locations, vertical travel distance (D), asymmetry angle (A), lifting frequency (F) and the quality of the hand-load coupling (Waters et al., 1993, 1994).

Table 1 shows the L values and the values of the chosen parameters and the corresponding values of the multipliers for each lifting risk condition (Fig. 1). The hand-to-object coupling was defined “good” for all the lifting tasks.

Before formal measurements were started, subjects underwent a training session to become familiar with the assessment procedures and ensure correct execution of the lifting tasks. Subjects also performed two repetitions of a specific exercise (Vera-Garcia et al., 2010) that were needed to record the isometric maximum voluntary contractions (iMVCs) for each of the investigated muscles according to SENIAM recommendations (Hermens et al., 2000).
Each subject was required to perform 18 trials (3 repetitions of each lifting task and risk condition).
The lifting trials were randomly assigned to each subject.

weight limit (RWL). LC was defined as 23 kg in RNLE. The values of Lifting Index (LI) were also reported.

A calibration procedure (spatial accuracy of 0.2 mm) was executed before the first data capture, to define a global reference system, (Wu et al., 2005). A global reference system (GRS) with the Y as vertical axis, X pointing in the antero-posterior direction and Z in the medio-lateral direction was adopted. Kinematic, ground reaction forces and moments and sEMG data were recorded (see Table 2).
Ground reaction forces and moments (force platform)

The movements of 37 spherical markers (15 mm in diameter) covered with aluminum powder reflective material were detected using an optoelectronic motion analysis system (SMART-DX 6000 System, BTS, Milan, Italy) with eight infrared cameras at 340 Hz sampling frequency. The markers were placed over prominent anatomical bony landmarks according to the International Society of Biomechanics recommendations (Wu et al., 2002, 2005) and to upper and lower limb and trunk biomechanical models (Davis et al., 1991, Gutierrez-Farewik et al., 2006, Rab et al., 2002; see Figure 1). In particular, the markers were placed bilaterally over the cutaneous projections of the metatarsal head, lateral malleoli, heel, fibula head, lateral femoral condyle, great trochanter, anterior superior iliac spine, head of the third metacarpal bone, ulnar styloid and radial processes, olecranon, acromion, posterior-superior parietal bone, and temple. Other markers were placed over the sacrum, T10, sternum, suprasternal notch (between the clavicular notches) and c7. Four additional markers were also placed over the vertexes of the load (a plastic crate).

Two force platforms (P 6000, BTS, Milan, Italy), embedded in the floor, with a sampling frequency of 680Hz, were used to acquire foot ground reaction forces, center of pressure (CoP) and moment (M) from the right and left legs.

Surface myoelectric signals were acquired at a sampling rate of 1000 Hz using a 16-channel Wi-Fi transmission surface electromyograph (FreeEMG300 System, BTS, Milan, Italy). After skin preparation, bipolar Ag/AgCl surface electrodes (2-cm diameter and interelectrode distance, H124SG Kendall ARBO, Tyco Healthcare, Neustadt/Donau, Germany) prepared with electroconductive gel were placed according to the European Recommendations for Surface Electromyography (Hermens et al., 2000) and the Atlas of Muscle Innervation Zones (Barbero et al., 2012): bilaterally on the erector spinae longissimus (ESL), erector spinae iliocostalis (ESI), multifidus (M), latissimus dorsi (LD), internal oblique (IO) and external oblique (EO) rectus abdominis superior (RAS) and rectus abdominis middle (RAM) muscles. The first four muscles were chosen because of their role as trunk extensors, the last four because of their role as flexors.

After acquisition, data were processed using Smart Analyzer (BTS) and Matlab (version 8.0.0.783; MathWorks, Natick, MA, USA) software. The vertical displacement and velocity of the marker placed over the vertex of the crate were calculated. Velocities were computed using finite difference derivatives and low-pass Butterworth filtered at a 4-Hz cut-off frequency. We ensured that the crate marker vertical displacement did not exceed D by more than 5% of the assigned value for each lifting task. The onset (event of start) of the lifting task was defined as the time point at which the crate marker vertical velocity exceeded a velocity threshold of 0.025 m/s (Ranavolo et al., 2015) on the vertical axis. Termination of the lifting task was defined as the maximum point on the graph of the vertical displacement (stop). Termination of the lowering phase (stop_lowering) was defined as the point on the graph at which the crate marker velocity fell below the velocity threshold in the opposite direction (Figure 2).
